summary: This program defines a makeCoffee function that takes two arguments — the drink type and the number of espresso shots — and calls it twice with different values. Inside, a small calculation decides whether the coffee earns a bonus message, showing how a function can hold logic as well as printing.

lines.text: Calls the function with two arguments: the text "Espresso" and the number 2. The order matters, because the first value fills the first parameter and the second fills the second.
Reusing the same function with different arguments is the whole point of parameters: one definition, many results.

lines.code: static void makeCoffee(String type, int shots) {
lines.text: Declares the function's two parameters with their types, so the compiler knows type holds text and shots holds a whole number. void means the function prints its results rather than handing a value back.

lines.code: System.out.println("🔮 Brewing " + type + " with " + shots + " shot(s)...");
lines.text: Joining text and variables with + builds one message, and Java automatically converts the number in shots into characters for printing.
Turns the incoming argument into a new value, which is what makes the function more than a printer — it computes something from its input.
A comparison produces either true or false, and storing that in a boolean gives the condition a readable name.
The block below runs only when the boolean is true, so two shots (84 magic power) earn the boost while one shot (42) does not.
Printing nothing leaves a blank line, which separates the output of the two calls so each coffee reads as its own block.
